human_tolerance.notes: The most abundant landbird in North America (370 million individuals, Partners in Flight 2019). 'The species is not shy about nesting close to human habitations', and in urban areas robins gather in numbers soon after lawns are mowed or where sprinklers are in use; they are also a common pest of fruit orchards. flight_distance_m and light_max are judgement, not separately sourced numbers.

phases.name: flocking
phases.note: Most robins depart south by the end of August and are back on the winter grounds from southern Canada to central Mexico and along the Pacific coast, assembling in large flocks at night to roost in trees in secluded swamps or dense vegetation. The flocks break up during the day to feed on fruits and berries in smaller groups.

phases.name: territorial
phases.note: Return north begins in February and March, exact dates varying with latitude and climate. Males defend a breeding territory and are less social during the summer.

phases.name: breeding
phases.note: One of the first North American birds to lay eggs, with two to three broods per breeding season over April to July. Clutches of three to five cyan eggs are incubated by the female alone; the eggs hatch after 14 days and the chicks leave the nest a further two weeks later. A new nest is built for each brood.

phases.name: moult
phases.note: Post-breeding moult before or during the southward movement; the source does not date it explicitly, so the window is aligned to the end of the breeding season.

vocalizations.description: The male's song is 'a complex and almost continuous song... commonly described as a cheery carol, made up of discrete units, often repeated, and spliced together into a string with brief pauses in between'. It varies regionally and by time of day, and is usually sung from a high perch in a tree. Robins are often among the first songbirds to sing as dawn rises, and last as evening sets in.

The source describes a set of calls 'used for communicating specific information, such as when a ground predator approaches and when a nest or another American robin is being directly threatened', used even in the competitive territorial period of the nesting season, when robins may band together to drive a predator away. The source does not name or transcribe this call, so it is recorded here by function rather than by imitation.

external.note: GBIF usage key, authorship and order from the GBIF Backbone Taxonomy; the iNaturalist taxa API matched taxon 12727 to 'American Robin'; ITIS TSN and NCBI taxon id from Wikidata (P815, P685).

range.note: Country and state list derived from Distribution and habitat: 'breeds throughout most of North America, from Alaska and Canada southward to northern Florida and Mexico', wintering 'from southern Canada to central Mexico and along the Pacific Coast', plus the Bermuda and Bahamas wintering range and the subspecies accounts. An approximation of the range, not an exhaustive one. No elevation range is given in the source, so elevation_m is omitted.

traits.note: Covers the structural traits (body plan, limb count, thermoregulation, skin, flight, respiration, metamorphosis, perching) and locomotion modes. The species 'forage[s] primarily on the ground', 'frequently seen running across lawns' and 'take[s] several short hops', with powered flight between winter roosts and the breeding range; The source describes the robin running and stopping across lawns as a distinguishing characteristic, but the biped_winged body plan has no run animation, so Walk and Hop carry ground foraging. Individual numeric and behavioural traits below carry their own entries.

traits.nest_type.note: 'The outer foundation consists of long coarse grass, twigs, paper, and feathers. This is lined with smeared mud and cushioned with fine grass or other soft materials' in a bush or tree fork - a mud-lined cup nest.

traits.size_class.note: From mass_kg (~0.08 kg); the validator's size-class bands place this in the Small band.

traits.mass_kg.note: 'The species averages about 77 g in weight' - a directly stated figure, not a derived midpoint. Wikidata P2067 carries the same 77.3 g.

traits.mass_range_kg.note: Full span across sexes: females 59-91 g, males 72-94 g.

traits.length_m.note: Midpoint of 23-28 cm for the eastern subspecies (T. m. migratorius), with similar size ranges across all subspecies.

traits.wingspan_m.note: Midpoint of the stated 31-41 cm range, as a direct conversion of the sourced wingspan rather than an inferred value.

traits.lifespan_y.note: 'Bird banders have found that only 25% of young robins survive their first year. The longest known lifespan of an American robin in the wild is 14 years; the average lifespan is about two years.' The average is used because it is the species' typical figure; the record maximum is recorded here.

traits.diet.note: Directly sourced: 'The diet generally consists of around 40 percent small invertebrates (mainly insects)... and 60 percent wild and cultivated fruits and berries.'

traits.social.note: 'During the summer, males defend a breeding territory and are less social', and 'the species is not shy about nesting close to human habitations'. The source does not state pair duration explicitly; a Pair breeding unit is inferred from territory defence by males, eggs incubated by the female alone and chicks fed by both parents. Non-breeding birds flock.

traits.activity_pattern.note: 'The American robin is active mostly during the day, and on its winter grounds, it assembles in large flocks at night to roost in trees.'

traits.defense.note: Judgement: the source describes vigilance in feeding flocks and collective driving away of predators while nesting, but the shared perching-songbird program responds to a close threat by moving away, so Flee was authored rather than Mob.

traits.wariness.note: Judgement: robins nest close to human habitations and feed on mown lawns, but flush readily from a close approach - a low-to-middling value for a garden bird.

habitat.note: Covers shelter_tag and habitat.resources. Invertebrate, fruit and berry tags come from the Diet section; nest_cup from the Breeding section (nest in a dense bush or tree fork) and perch from singing 'from a high perch in a tree'. Weights are judgement, not separately sourced percentages.

habitat.use.note: 'Robins forage primarily on the ground for soft-bodied invertebrates, and find worms by sight... pouncing on them and then pulling them up', 'frequently seen running across lawns'; trees are used for nesting, high song perches and communal winter roosts.

habitat.human_tolerance.note: Breeding and Diet sections: 'The species is not shy about nesting close to human habitations', 'In urban areas, robins will gather in numbers soon after lawns are mowed or where sprinklers are in use', 'American robins are common pests of fruit orchards in North America'. Abundance from the lead (Partners in Flight 2019, 370 million). flight_distance_m and light_max are judgement, not separately sourced numbers.

seasonal.strategy.note: 'While robins occasionally overwinter in the northern part of the United States and southern Canada, most migrate to winter south of Canada from Florida and the Gulf Coast to central Mexico, as well as along the Pacific Coast.' A partial migrant rather than a wholly migratory one, so PartialMigration was used.

seasonal.phases.note: Winter flocking and roosting, February-March return and summer territoriality, breeding from April to July with two to three broods and the quoted clutch, incubation and nestling figures. The moult window is the one judgement here: the source does not date the post-breeding moult, so it is aligned to the end of the breeding season and labelled as such. The breeding phase is tagged US-CO because the locale that prompted this record is in Colorado; the source's dates are continental.

seasonal.life_stages.note: Egg (three to five cyan eggs), altricial juvenile (naked with eyes closed for the first few days, leaving the nest two weeks after hatching, capable of sustained flight two weeks after fledging, sexually mature at one year, only 25% surviving the first year) and adult. No sourced juvenile-plumage duration was found, so duration_days is unset and the juvenile scale is judgement.

vocalizations.song.note: Vocalization section: 'a complex and almost continuous song... commonly described as a cheery carol, made up of discrete units, often repeated', sung from a high perch, 'among the first songbirds to sing as dawn rises' and last into the evening. season_months 3-7 follows the stated song period of late February or early March to late July or early August.

vocalizations.alarm.note: Vocalization section: calls used 'when a ground predator approaches and when a nest or another American robin is being directly threatened'. The source names no transcription for this call, so it is recorded by function only; loudness and cooldown are judgement.

look.note: Description section: 'The head varies from jet black to gray, with white eye arcs and white supercilia. The throat is white with black streaks, and the belly and undertail coverts are white. The adult has a brown back and a reddish-orange breast, varying from a rich red maroon to peachy orange. The bill is mainly yellow with a variably dark tip... and the legs and feet are brown.' Palette places the orange-red on the breast part and the brown back on the body, with the yellow bill as the accent; proportions are authored judgement.

behavior.note: Authored parameters for the shared perching-songbird program: food_tag is the invertebrate share, which the program uses for ground foraging; flee_m and wariness reflect a bird that is tolerant of people but flushes readily; nest_m1/nest_m2 span the stated April-July breeding season.
